plan: [Assume other bidders bid their true values. In a 3rd-price auction with 5 bidders, winning probability = (b/49)^4 and conditional expected payment = 0.6b. Expected profit = (b/49)^4*(34 - 0.6b). Maximizing gives b = 136/3 ≈ 45.33. Because the price is the 3rd-highest, overbidding is optimal here. Round to the nearest $0.1.]

[Third-price auction with 5 bidders incentivizes systematic overbidding. Assume symmetric linear bids b(v)=αv. With 4 opponents, probability win if bidding as-if t is t^4 and expected third-price (second-highest of 4 others) conditional on max<t is (3/5)t, so payoff ∝ t^4(v - α*(3/5)t). First-order condition gives best-response t=4v/(3α). Symmetry implies α=4/3, so equilibrium b(v)=(4/3)v. For v=$28, bid = (4/3)*28 = $37.333…, round to nearest $0.1 = $37.3.]

[Assume other bidders bid their values (uniform 0–49). If I bid b and win (all 4 others < b), win prob = (b/49)^4. If I win I pay the second-highest of the other four; for uniforms on [0,b] its expectation = 3/5 b = 0.6b. Expected payoff = (b/49)^4*(14 - 0.6b). Maximizing gives b* = 56/3 ≈ 18.667. With 0.1 increments, I will bid 18.7 to maximize long-run expected profit under these assumptions.]

[With five bidders and third-price payment, there is strong incentive to shade bids below value. I approximate the symmetric equilibrium multiplier for a 3rd-price, 5-player auction as (k-1)/(n-1)=2/4=0.5. Bidding half my private value balances winning probability against overpaying and maximizes long-run expected profit under iid draws. Value = $14, so bid 0.5*14 = $7.0. This is cautious, consistent across rounds, and robust given no history here.]

[Value = $40. With no history and independent draws, bid my true value to maximize probability of winning when value is high. In a third-price auction the winner pays the third-highest bid, typically well below my value with four opponents, so bidding 40 is a robust, profit-maximizing choice for this single round.
